name: Low-carb diet

image.caption: LOW CARB KETO FRIED CHICKEN by Keto Diet Delish Medium

lead: A low-carb diet cuts bread, sugar, pasta and starches and relies more on meat, fish, eggs, dairy, nuts and non-starchy vegetables. People use it to lose body fat, sharpen their physique and, some say, clear their skin. It is often positioned between ordinary eating and stricter carnivore regimens.

There is no single definition: one professional body treats under 20 percent of energy from carbohydrate as low-carb, another uses under 25 percent, and ketogenic versions go below about 50 grams a day. Trials generally find slightly more weight loss than low-fat diets in the short and medium term, with the gap shrinking over time, and long-term results track calorie intake and adherence. Higher protein may increase fullness. Forum users disagree, with some reporting hunger, low energy and weaker gym performance while others tolerate it well.

paras: People swap starches for protein, fats and vegetables, often with higher protein to help keep muscle while cutting. Early loss is partly water, and fat loss follows over weeks to months. Many use a moderate version rather than ketogenic levels.

Reported side effects include constipation, headache, bad breath, cramps and weakness. Long-term cohort data are mixed, and cardiology and dietetic bodies advise discussing very low-carb versions with a clinician. Ketoacidosis is rare but documented, mostly in diabetes.

chain: Lower calorie intake, less water weight
angle.text: Users cut carbohydrates to lower calorie intake and body fat for a leaner physique, sometimes pairing it with high protein to keep muscle. Trials show slightly faster early weight loss than low-fat diets, with the gap narrowing over time.

lead: A low-carbohydrate diet restricts carbohydrate intake relative to typical Western eating, usually limiting sugars, bread, pasta and starches and relying more on meat, fish, eggs, dairy, nuts and non-starchy vegetables. There is no standard definition: one professional body treats under 20 percent of energy from carbohydrate as low-carb, another uses under 25 percent, and ketogenic variants typically go below about 50 grams a day.[1] This makes studies difficult to compare.

In looksmaxxing communities the diet is discussed as a way to reduce body fat, improve skin and manage energy, and it is often positioned between ordinary eating and stricter carnivore regimens. Forum users hold opposing views, with some reporting that cutting carbohydrate left them hungry, fatigued and with poor training performance.[2]

Published research generally finds that low-carb diets produce slightly more weight loss than low-fat diets in the short and medium term, with the difference small and diminishing over time; long-term outcomes appear to depend largely on calorie intake and adherence.[1] Major health bodies differ in how they position the approach.
infobox: Roughly under 20 to 25 percent of energy from carbohydrate; no universal standard
Often under about 50 g carbohydrate per day
John Rollo (1797), William Banting (1863), Robert Atkins (1972)

paras: Low-carb diets replace refined and starchy carbohydrate with foods higher in protein and fat. Non-starchy vegetables are usually retained.[1] Intensity ranges from mild reduction (around 40 percent of energy from carbohydrate in one 2016 classification) to very low intakes of about 50 grams a day, and the modified Atkins pattern can be under 10 grams a day.[1]

Popular named plans such as the Zone and South Beach diets are sometimes marketed as low-carb but have been described as closer to moderate carbohydrate intake.[1] Ketogenic diets and carnivore-style diets sit at the stricter end of the spectrum.

In 1797 the British surgeon John Rollo treated diabetic army officers with a low-carbohydrate regimen, and very low-carbohydrate eating was the standard diabetes treatment through the nineteenth century.[1] In 1863 William Banting, an English undertaker, published a booklet describing his weight loss after cutting bread, butter, milk, sugar, beer and potatoes; the word banting entered popular use for dieting.[1]

Robert Atkins's Dr. Atkins' Diet Revolution (1972) was a commercial success but was criticised by mainstream medical bodies; popularity peaked in the late 1990s and early 2000s, with some estimates of up to 18 percent of Americans using such diets.[1]

Reviews report that low-carb diets often lead to slightly greater weight loss than low-fat diets in the short and medium term, an advantage described as small and equivalent to roughly 100 kilocalories a day that fades over time.[1] A 2022 Cochrane review found no benefit over balanced diets at two years.[1]

The carbohydrate-insulin hypothesis, promoted by Gary Taubes and David Ludwig, predicted a large metabolic advantage for low-carb eating; a well-funded test did not confirm this, and researcher Kevin Hall concluded the hypothesis had been falsified by that experiment, according to the Wikipedia summary.[1] Proponents of the hypothesis continue to dispute such interpretations.
Protein, which tends to rise on low-carb diets, has been reviewed as supporting satiety, preservation of fat-free mass and maintenance of energy expenditure during weight loss.[3]

In type 2 diabetes, carbohydrate restriction often improves blood glucose control, though weight loss is not consistently better, and some guidance accepts reduced-carbohydrate options for people who cannot reach glucose targets.[1] A small study found that carbohydrate restriction combined with walking after meals reduced post-meal glucose spikes and improved endothelial function in type 2 diabetes.[4]

For liver fat, a comparison of low-fat and low-carb interventions found that common liver fat scores tracked changes in liver fat under a low-fat diet but not under a low-carb diet.[5] A review of dietary strategies for fatty liver disease discusses carbohydrate restriction among several approaches.[6]

Ketogenic diets, the strictest form, have been reviewed as a possible therapy for mood disorders, with the authors describing the evidence base as developing,[7] and a pilot experience reported possible benefit in refractory migraine.[8]

Commonly reported effects include constipation, headache, bad breath, muscle cramps and weakness.[1] Ketosis is a normal metabolic state, but ketoacidosis, a rare and potentially life-threatening condition, has been reported in case reports with Atkins and South Beach diets.[1] Very restrictive versions risk fibre and micronutrient shortfalls, and rare case reports describe thiamine-deficiency encephalopathy, optic neuropathy and other complications.[1]

Cohort evidence on long-term use is mixed. Diets followed for under two years did not worsen cardiovascular markers in reviews cited by Wikipedia, whereas long-term adherence has been associated with higher total and LDL cholesterol, and one study linked it to higher cardiovascular mortality.[1] A large Japanese cohort associated high adherence with higher overall cancer risk, attributed mainly to animal rather than plant sources of fat.[1]
Low-carb diets may reduce capacity for high-intensity exercise and slow muscle glycogen recovery.[1]

The US National Academy of Medicine sets an average recommended intake of 130 grams of carbohydrate a day, and the FAO and WHO recommend that most dietary energy come from carbohydrate.[1] The UK NHS describes carbohydrate as the body's main energy source.[1]

The American College of Cardiology advises discussion with a clinician before very low-carb diets and notes possible long-term LDL increases; the American Heart Association (2021) found insufficient evidence that ketogenic diets promote heart health; and the American Diabetes Association treats reduced-carb eating as one viable approach for some people with type 2 diabetes.[1] The British Dietetic Association listed the ketogenic diet among its worst celebrity diets in 2018.[1]

Many randomised trials and meta-analyses of low-carb diets exist, mainly for weight loss, diabetes and epilepsy, and their conclusions are summarised above. Wikipedia notes that many lower-quality meta-analyses favoured low-carb diets, a pattern that may reflect publication bias, while higher-quality reviews show little difference.[1] No trial has studied low-carb diets specifically for facial appearance or attractiveness.

Small studies cover related questions, including carbohydrate restriction in women with breast cancer, which reported improvements in quality of life and body composition,[9] and a mouse study of a low-carbohydrate, high-protein diet in prostate tumours.[10]

On looksmax.org, discussions about carbohydrates sit alongside carnivore and animal-based diet threads. One widely replied thread argues against low-carb eating, with its author describing constant hunger, low energy, poor mood and low libido after one to two months of very low carbohydrate intake despite eating eggs, liver and chicken, and recommending lower-glycaemic carbohydrate sources instead.[2] Other users report fat loss and appetite control on reduced-carbohydrate diets in related threads.

lore.intro: Low-carb eating is discussed on looksmax.org both as a leanness tool and as a diet some users say left them depleted.[2]
